analysis.one_liner: Gives college athletes a federal right to earn money from their name, image, and likeness.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2021 with zero cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing, a vote, or floor action before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written into federal law a right for college athletes — including high schoolers being recruited — to make money from their name, image, likeness, and athletic fame. It barred the NCAA, conferences, and universities from enforcing rules against that, barred them from colluding to cap what athletes could be paid, protected athletes' right to hire agents and lawyers, and allowed athletes to form collective representatives for group licensing. It backed the right with Federal Trade Commission enforcement, private lawsuits with attorney's fees, and automatic antitrust liability, and it overrode state NIL laws.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes and even recruited high school players, who gain an enforceable federal right to earn endorsement and licensing income without jeopardizing scholarships. Athletes could also hire professional representation freely and form collective bodies to negotiate group licensing deals — a channel that has historically benefited only professional athletes in major sports.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a federal right for college and prospective college athletes to market their name, image, likeness, and athletic reputation, and prohibits colleges and athletic associations from enacting or enforcing rules that prevent it [S2][S3].
Bars colleges, conferences, and third parties from coordinating to limit the payment offered to athletes, and makes violations a per se Sherman Act antitrust violation [S3].
Protects athletes' ability to retain agents, financial advisors, and attorneys, and forbids schools and associations from regulating that representation [S2][S3].

Allows athletes to form collective representatives for group licensing, and requires third parties to license from the group before using any member's NIL, while guaranteeing NIL earnings cannot affect scholarship eligibility or amounts [S3].
Enforces the rights through the FTC, private lawsuits with damages and attorney's fees for prevailing athletes, and antitrust remedies [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The NCAA, athletic conferences, and university athletic departments, which lose their authority to restrict athlete compensation and would face FTC enforcement and antitrust suits for colluding to cap athlete pay. Advertisers and licensees also pay athletes directly for endorsements, and institutions would bear the cost of providing marketing support equitably across sports and genders.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state NIL laws, replacing a patchwork of state rules with a single federal regime that states could not supplement or tailor [S3].

It grants marketability rights, not pay: earnings flow through endorsements and licensing, which tend to concentrate in high-profile sports and star athletes, and the bill addresses resulting gaps by gender, race, and sport mainly through grants to study them rather than through guarantees [S3].
Enforcement depends on the FTC and on athletes suing in federal court, so individual athletes with less bargaining power or legal help may find the right hard to use in practice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For college athletes, the bill offered the strongest version of NIL rights that appeared in Congress: a hard federal floor, anti-collusion teeth backed by antitrust law, and collective bargaining-style group licensing. The costs fall almost entirely on the college sports establishment, which generates billions in revenue from unpaid labor; that is the point of the bill, not a hidden cost. The genuine weaknesses are its one-size-fits-all preemption of state law and the fact that market-driven earnings would likely flow unevenly across sports and genders — a problem the bill studies but does not solve.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce Committee from February 2021 until Congress ended in January 2023, never getting a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on February 4, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1][S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor during the entire session [S4].
No further action of any kind was taken after the referral — no committee report, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history before the 117th Congress ended [S5].

In July 2021, without any federal law, the NCAA adopted an interim policy allowing college athletes in all divisions to profit from their name, image, and likeness, which changed the on-the-ground landscape while leaving the bill's stronger protections — anti-collusion enforcement, group licensing rights, and collective representation — unenacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: College sports institutions came out ahead. The NCAA, conferences, and university athletic departments never faced federal anti-collusion rules, FTC enforcement, or per se antitrust liability for limiting athlete pay; athletes instead received only what the NCAA's own interim policy and state laws permitted.

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the College Athlete Economic Freedom Act in the Senate on February 4, 2021.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to; chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D)
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record after the February 2021 referral.

against.name: The other 99 senators
against.role: Colleagues who never signed on as cosponsors
against.what_they_did: None joined as a cosponsor during the two-year session, leaving the bill with no demonstrated support for committee or floor action.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat, but no senator of either party signed on as a cosponsor in the two years the bill was pending [S4], so no party split ever formed.

industries.industry: College sports institutions (NCAA, conferences, athletic departments)
industries.note: The bill strips their authority to bar athletes from endorsement income, forbids them from coordinating to cap athlete pay, and exposes such coordination to per se antitrust liability. Their revenue model historically depended on athletes who could not sell their own name, image, or likeness [S2][S3].

The bill opens a large pool of athlete endorsements and requires group licensing from athletes before their NIL is used in collective marketing, creating new paid inventory for brands while guaranteeing athletes are compensated [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Athlete agents and financial and legal representatives
industries.note: The bill forbids colleges and associations from regulating or certifying athlete representation, expanding agents' and advisors' ability to serve college athletes without school gatekeeping [S2][S3].
